question.text: Per NISM Ch 2.2 on Traditional Investments, which statement correctly contrasts equity shares and debt instruments?

answer.text: Equity shareholders are senior claimants over debt holders in a liquidation waterfall.
Both equity and debt carry identical voting rights and identical payment priorities.
Debt instruments always pay higher returns than equity because they carry higher risk.

Equity shares represent ownership with residual claim on profits after contractual claims are satisfied and carry voting rights; debt instruments are contracts promising a stream of cashflows with contractual restrictions on the borrower and defined rights on default.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Chapter 2.2.1, equity shareholders 'are residual owners of firm's profit after other contractual claims on the firm are satisfied and they have the ultimate control over how the firm is operated'. Per 2.2.2, debt is 'a promise to pay a stream of cashflows during the term of the contract... establishes the financial requirements and restrictions that the borrower must meet and the rights of the holder of the debt instruments if the borrower defaults'. The Trap: Option A inverts the capital-structure waterfall (debt is senior). Option C is factually false — debt carries no voting, equity holders are residual. Option D is wrong both directions — debt typically has LOWER expected return because it has LOWER risk. Cross-Exam Context: X-A (IA L1), XV (RA), and XXI-B (PM) all test the equity-vs-debt primitive in various framings. XIX-C tests it as the foundation for understanding why PE (equity-like) and private credit (debt-like) sit in different AIF sub-strategies. Manager's Pro-Tip: In a hybrid Cat II AIF that does mezzanine, the IC memo should explicitly tag each instrument as senior secured / sub / preference / equity — LPs compute expected loss using this waterfall, and a single mis-tag in your portfolio report triggers an audit question.
